content: # St. Lucia Harsewinkel. ## St. Lucia. St. Lucia in Harsewinkel, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, is an architectural gem and a symbol of the town's rich historical tapestry. This Catholic parish church, with its towering spire and intricate neo-Gothic design, stands as a testament to centuries of faith, craftsmanship, and community spirit. ### The History of St. Lucia. The first documented mention of Harsewinkel's church dates back to approximately 1050 in a record from the Freckenhorst Monastery, referring to it as Haswinklia. The church's dedication to St. Lucia suggests a historical link to the church in Warendorf. In the early 12th century, the Wadenhart Chapel was established in the nearby community of Hundingen, now Marienfeld, as an extension of St. Lucia. The architectural history of St. Lucia is as rich and varied as its spiritual heritage. ### The Community and St. Lucia. In conclusion, St. Lucia in Harsewinkel is more than just a church; it is a symbol of the town's rich heritage and a beacon of faith and community spirit.

Southwest Germany is blessed with a treasure trove of more than 60 old monasteries, palaces, and castles that you can visit and explore. ### Salem Monastery and Palace. The former Cistercian abbey at Salem is one of the most important cultural heritage sites in the Lake Constance region – and one of the most beautiful. Salem Monastery and Palace (Kloster und Schloss Salem) is a singular combination of Gothic solemnity and Baroque splendor. You can hear the Salem organ during regular services, organ recitals and as part of the Salem Monastery Concerts.

title: Archaeologists discover 600-year-old Christian monastery in Germany
content: The thick monastery walls were preserved beneath rubble that collected over the centuries. A development project in the town center of Borken, in western Germany, revealed the well-preserved remains of a monastery. The brick foundation was over five feet tall in some places, and it was buried under thick layers of rubble. Archaeologists working on a preventive dig ahead of a construction project in the German town of Borken, near the Dutch border, discovered a remarkable piece of history. The red brick foundations and thick walls of the church, which were bound by lime mortar, are well-preserved despite the passing of the centuries. The walls were four feet thick and over five feet tall, often buried beneath layers of thick rubble that helped preserve the ancient foundation as the city grew and expanded over it.
